hello.note: Casual: Salom. The reply is Vaalaykum assalom.

goodbye.note: More polite: Xayr, salomat boʻling ('goodbye, stay well').

please.note: Goes before or after the request: Iltimos, suv bering or Suv bering, iltimos ('Water, please').

thank_you.note: Thank you very much: Katta rahmat. More formal: Tashakkur.

youre_welcome.note: Literally 'it's not worth it'. Also heard: Sogʻ boʻling ('be healthy').

yes.note: Agreeing to a request: Xoʻp ('all right').

sorry.note: Kechirasiz is just as common. More formal: Uzr soʻrayman ('I apologise').

excuse_me.note: People often add aka (to a man) or opa (to a woman): Kechirasiz, aka!

good_morning.note: In practice many people simply say Assalomu alaykum at any time of day.

how_are_you.note: Also very common: Yaxshimisiz? ('Are you well?'). To a friend: Qalaysan?

im_fine.note: Then ask back: Oʻzingiz qalaysiz? ('And how are you?')

whats_your_name.note: Extra polite: Ismingizni bilsam boʻladimi? ('May I know your name?')

im_from.note: The ending -dan attaches to the country: Men Fransiyadanman ('I'm from France').

speak_english.note: Also very natural: Ingliz tilini bilasizmi? ('Do you know English?')

dont_understand.note: Literally 'I didn't understand' — the usual way to say it in the moment.

where.note: Where to? is Qayerga? and where from? is Qayerdan?

what.note: To politely ask someone to repeat, say Labbay? instead.

how_much.note: At the bazaar people usually just say: Necha pul?

where_bathroom.note: In everyday speech Tualet qayerda? is very common.

one.note: When counting things people say bitta: bitta choy ('one tea').

tea.note: Green tea: koʻk choy. Black tea: qora choy.

im_hungry.note: Literally 'my stomach is hungry'. Also common: Qornim ochdi.

delicious.note: On first tasting something: Mazali ekan! ('it's tasty!')

enjoy_meal.note: Osh boʻlsin! is said to someone eating or who has just finished.

left.note: Chap is 'left'; chapga means 'to the left', as in directions.

right.note: Oʻng is 'right'; oʻngga means 'to the right', as in directions.

stop_here.note: Also very natural: Shu yerda toʻxtatib bering.

want_to_go.note: -ga attaches to the place: Samarqandga. After k it becomes -ka, after q -qa.

one_ticket.note: Bitta, not bir, is used when counting things.

too_expensive.note: At the bazaar, Qimmat-ku! is a good way to start bargaining.

pay_card.note: Also heard: Terminal bormi? ('Is there a card terminal?')

cash.note: Often just naqd: Naqd toʻlayman ('I'll pay cash').

yesterday.note: Kecha also means 'night'; context makes it clear.

see_you_later.note: Also: Keyin koʻrishamiz ('we'll see each other later').

wait_moment.note: In speech often just: Bir minut!

call_police.note: Politsiya is also understood. Police emergency number: 102.

need_doctor.note: In speech also vrach or doktor.

allergic.note: -ga attaches to the allergen; after q it becomes -qa: yeryongʻoqqa ('to peanuts').

no_problem.note: Agreeing to a request: Bemalol ('go ahead, no problem').

i_like_it.note: About something you've just seen or tried: Menga yoqdi.

dont_like_it.note: About something you've just seen or tried: Menga yoqmadi.

welcome.note: At the door you will also hear: Keling, marhamat! ('come in, please').

congratulations.note: For weddings, a new baby or holidays: Muborak boʻlsin!

my_family.note: Shorter and very common: Oilam. The ending -m means 'my'.

mother.note: Calling your own mum: oyi (aya in some regions). Affectionate: onajon.

father.note: Calling your own dad: dada. Affectionate: otajon.

brother.note: Aka is an older brother (and a polite way to address any man). A younger brother is uka.

sister.note: Opa is an older sister (and a polite way to address any woman). A younger sister is singil.

child.note: Son: oʻgʻil. Daughter: qiz. In everyday speech bola ('child, kid') is also used.

friend.note: Same word for men and women. Also common: oʻrtoq. A woman's female friend is often dugona.

this_is_my_friend.note: A woman introducing a female friend often says: Bu mening dugonam.

are_you_married.note: Also common: Oilalimisiz? To a man: Uylanganmisiz? To a woman: Turmushga chiqqanmisiz?

monday.note: Days are not capitalised. On Monday: dushanba kuni.

tuesday.note: Du-, se-, chor-, pay- are the Persian numbers 2–5 (pay- from panj) joined to shanba.

friday.note: The day of the Friday prayer. On Friday: juma kuni.

sunday.note: Yak- is Persian for 'one': the first day after shanba.

weekend.note: Literally 'rest days'. Also heard: hafta oxiri ('end of the week').

what_day.note: Asking the date instead: Bugun nechanchi sana?

next_week.note: Also common: keyingi hafta. Last week: oʻtgan hafta.

eleven.note: Teens are oʻn ('ten') + the unit: oʻn bir, oʻn ikki, oʻn uch…

twenty.note: Tens + unit, no 'and': yigirma bir (21), yigirma besh (25).

fifty.note: Forty: qirq. Sixty: oltmish. Seventy: yetmish. Eighty: sakson. Ninety: toʻqson.

hundred.note: Yuz also means 'face'. Two hundred: ikki yuz. In formal writing (e.g. sums in contracts): bir yuz.

thousand.note: Prices run into thousands: besh ming soʻm (5,000 soʻm).

years_old.note: The number goes before yoshdaman: Men oʻttiz yoshdaman.

blue.note: Koʻk is also used for green plants and tea: koʻk choy is green tea. Sky blue: havorang.

white.note: Oq yoʻl! ('white road') is how you wish someone a good journey.

this_one.note: To ask for it: Bunisini bering.

that_one.note: Colloquial: anavi. To ask for it: Unisini bering.

its_hot.note: Very hot: Juda issiq! In speech often just: Issiq.

its_cold.note: If you yourself feel cold: Sovqotyapman.

its_sunny.note: Ochiq here means 'clear'. When the sun comes out: Quyosh chiqdi.

have_reservation.note: Also very common: Xona bron qilganman.

room.note: In hotels you will also hear nomer.

luggage.note: At the airport usually bagaj. A suitcase: chamadon.

check_out_time.note: Literally 'At what time must the room be vacated?'

is_this_seat_free.note: Also: Bu yerga oʻtirsam boʻladimi? ('May I sit here?')

what_do_you_do.note: Also common: Qayerda ishlaysiz? ('Where do you work?')

i_work_in.note: -da attaches to the place: Men bankda ishlayman. For a field: savdo sohasida ('in sales').

im_student.note: Same for men and women. A school pupil says: Men oʻquvchiman.

office.note: The Uzbek word idora is also used, especially for official institutions.

meeting.note: A formal meeting: majlis. Meeting a person: uchrashuv.

day_off.note: The plural, dam olish kunlari, means 'weekend'.

colleague.note: Same word for men and women.

table_for_two.note: Also natural: Ikki kishilik joy bormi? ('Is there a place for two?')

not_spicy.note: Achchiq means both spicy and bitter. Also: Qalampir solmang ('no chilli').

vegetarian_food.note: Goʻshtsiz ('without meat') is often clearer: Goʻshtsiz taom bormi?

im_full.note: Politely to a host: Rahmat, toʻydim.

takeaway.note: Also: Oʻrab bering ('wrap it up, please') or simply Olib ketaman ('I'll take it with me').

it_was_delicious.note: To the host or cook, add: Qoʻlingiz dard koʻrmasin! ('may your hands never ache').

keep_change.note: Also: Qaytimi qolsin ('let the change stay').

stomach.note: Qorin is the belly; the organ itself is oshqozon. My stomach: qornim.

have_fever.note: Also: Isitmam chiqdi ('I've got a temperature').

medicine.note: A pharmacy, dorixona, is literally 'medicine house'.

happy_birthday.note: To a friend: Tugʻilgan kuning bilan! Often followed by tabriklayman ('I congratulate you').

thanks_a_lot.note: Also: Koʻp rahmat. Even warmer: Juda katta rahmat!

miss_you.note: To an elder, or politely: Sizni sogʻindim.
